summary: This Environmental Protection Department page explains volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and how they contribute to smog and fine particulates in Hong Kong and the Pearl River Delta. It covers health effects of smog, where to find air quality information via the AQHI, the government's regulatory measures such as the VOC Regulation, and practical steps residents can take to reduce VOC emissions.
one_line: Explains how volatile organic compounds form smog in Hong Kong, its health effects, government VOC controls, and ways residents can reduce emissions.
key_facts: VOCs are found in solvent-based paints, printing inks, many consumer products, organic solvents and petroleum products, and motor vehicles and vessels also emit them.
Under sunlight, VOCs react with nitrogen oxides emitted mainly from vehicles, power plants and industrial activities to form ozone.
Smog is particularly severe under strong sunlight and stagnant weather conditions, such as a typhoon approaching or northerly winds common in autumn.
Smog can worsen existing heart and respiratory problems such as asthma.
People with heart and lung problems, the elderly and children whose respiratory systems are still developing are most at risk from smog.
Prolonged exposure to severe smog condition may cause permanent damage to lung tissue and affect the immune system.
The AQHI (Air Quality Health Index) reported by the EPD tells the latest and forecast short-term health risk of air pollution.

In April 1999 the government introduced a regulation under the Air Pollution Control Ordinance (APCO) requiring recovery of petrol vapour during petrol unloading at petrol filling stations, amended in March 2005 to extend recovery to vehicle refuelling.
The VOC Regulation has applied in phases since 1 April 2007 to architectural paints/coatings, printing inks and six selected consumer products.
The six selected consumer products are air fresheners, hairsprays, multi-purpose lubricants, floor wax strippers, insecticides and aerosol insect repellents.
The 2009 amendment extended controls from 1 January 2010 to vehicle refinishing paints/coatings, vessel and pleasure craft paints/coatings, adhesives and sealants.
In 2017 the regulation was amended to cover fountain solutions and printing machine cleaning agents with effect from 1 January 2018.
The government works with the Guangdong Provincial Government to set targets to jointly reduce VOC emissions in the Pearl River Delta region.
Residents are advised to avoid aerosol consumer products that often use VOCs as propellants and to replace solvent-based paints with water-based paints.
Thinners are almost 100% VOCs, so applying solvent-based products with hand brushes or rollers instead of sprayers reduces their use and minimizes overspray.
